title: Space out sign-ons while the host refuses them

blocks.text: The host's operators have written to you twice.

items: During last Tuesday's maintenance window your client sent them a sign-on every second for twenty minutes, and they would like that to stop.
After a night-long outage, when the host came back at 06:10, your client was among the clients that hammered it with sign-ons, though it had been quiet for most of the night.

blocks.text: Their rules of connection: after a refused or unanswered sign-on, wait `firstWait` before the next one, and twice as long after each further refusal in a row, but never longer than `longestWait`. After an accepted sign-on, the next outage starts afresh.

The sign-on manager asks `maySignOn(now)` before each sign-on and reports every outcome to `LinkPolicy` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/LinkPolicy.java`. Finish `refused` and `signedOn`, the two methods marked `TODO`. About eight lines in total. Times are milliseconds and the caller passes them in, so the tests play a whole night in a moment.

cases.says: after a refusal the next sign-on waits, and it may go out once the longest wait has passed
after an accepted sign-on nothing stops the next one
the first refusal of a series waits exactly the first wait, not twice it
each further refusal doubles the wait until it reaches the longest wait, which it never exceeds
after hundreds of refusals the wait is still the longest wait, never negative, zero or short again
a success ends the series, so the next outage starts again from the first wait

origin.section: 15.2.1 Spot the Problem: Doubling by Shifting

concepts: A refused sign-on is retried after a wait that doubles with each refusal in a row up to a cap and starts over after a success; the cap is also how long a link may stay out after its host recovers.
Doubling by shifting overflows after a few hours of refusals and the delay turns negative, zero or short; doubling step by step inside the cap cannot.
